name: Hydrolyzed keratin

lead: Hydrolyzed keratin is keratin protein, from sources such as feathers or wool, chopped into small fragments so it dissolves in water. It is added to conditioners and masks with claims of strengthening damaged hair.
A 120-person trial of a keratin peptide powder for hair health is registered as completed, but no results are posted. Most other published work is on non-cosmetic biomaterials.

paras: Proponents say small protein fragments can deposit on or fill gaps in damaged hair. The sources reviewed here do not include studies testing that mechanism in hair.
No hair-specific safety findings are described in the sources reviewed. It is an ordinary cosmetic ingredient; individual products vary.

lead: Hydrolyzed keratin is keratin, the structural protein of hair, wool, nails and feathers, that has been broken down into smaller peptide and amino-acid fragments so that it can dissolve in water. It is used as a protein ingredient in hair conditioners and similar products, where it is marketed for strengthening and repairing damaged hair.[1]

Native keratin is highly insoluble, largely because of disulfide bonds formed by the amino acid cysteine, and only certain reducing or dissolving agents can break it down.[1] Hydrolyzed forms are made from sources such as feathers and wool and have also been studied as biomaterials for tissue engineering, films and nanofibres.[2][3]

Published evidence for cosmetic hair benefits is thin. A registered trial of a hydrolyzed keratin peptide powder for hair health has been completed, but its results are not described in the registry record.[4]

paras: Keratin makes up hair, wool, nails, feathers and the outer layer of skin. Its toughness and insolubility come from cysteine-rich disulfide cross-links.[1] Hydrolysis cleaves the protein chain into fragments small enough to be mixed into water-based formulas.
Besides cosmetics, hydrolyzed keratin has appeared in laboratory work on electrospun scaffolds, biodegradable plastic blends, cross-linked films and flocculants.[2][3][5][6]

Manufacturers add hydrolyzed keratin to conditioners and treatments with claims of smoothing, strengthening and repairing damaged strands. These are product claims; the sources reviewed here do not provide controlled comparisons of such products.
The ingredient is also associated with keratin-based smoothing treatments, covered separately under keratin straightening.

A registered trial (NCT07458828, started January 2024, 120 participants, completed) evaluated the efficacy and safety of a hydrolyzed keratin peptide powder on hair damage, hair health and hair strength; the registry entry lists no published results.[4]

Other human work involves oral supplements combining hydrolyzed keratin with other ingredients for knee osteoarthritis, which is unrelated to appearance.[7] Most remaining literature is laboratory research on biomaterials.
